title: Nonlinear-gate advantages for binary linear operators
formal:
Can arbitrary Boolean gates give an unbounded wire saving over XOR gates for computing a binary linear operator? Determine whether
\[\forall K>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\setminus\{0\}:\quad
C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)>K\,C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A).\]
Both models allow unrestricted fan-in, fan-out and depth and must compute the entire same map \(x\mapsto Ax\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) on every input. GEN permits an arbitrary Boolean function at each gate and charges its incoming wires, not the gate's internal implementation. This adopts the unbounded-factor meaning of “help” made explicit by the constant-factor comparison following Problem 7.18.
why: The final map is linear, but a general circuit may pass through nonlinear intermediate values. The question asks whether such intermediate computation can ever save an unbounded number of wires relative to staying linear throughout. It tests a basic structural limitation of circuit computation over the two-element field, where familiar linearization statements from infinite-field settings cannot simply be imported.
status_note: Problem 7.18, Chapter 6 and the following comparison discussion were read on 2026-09-14. Ko’s arXiv:2509.02730v1 introduction, main-result discussion and Section 4.1 were checked for later-work scope. Its preprocessing and fixed-depth results do not settle the every-matrix unrestricted-depth ratio. A bounded search through this date did not locate a matching separation or constant-factor theorem. sentences: The problem asks whether nonlinear intermediate computation can save an unbounded number of wires when the final output map is linear over the two-element field.
The comparison is between XOR-only circuits and circuits with arbitrary Boolean gate functions.
Both have unrestricted depth and fan-in and must compute the same map exactly on every input.
Correctness only on basis vectors and results restricted to shallow circuits do not answer this question.
A positive answer establishes arbitrarily large savings, while a negative answer gives one simulation factor for every matrix.

definitions:
Let \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo two. For an integer \(n\ge1\), a matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) defines the total map \(x\mapsto Ax\) from \(\mathbb F_2^n\) to itself, with \((Ax)_i=\bigoplus_{j:a_{ij}=1}x_j\). An empty XOR is zero.

Both types of circuit are finite directed acyclic graphs with distinct input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and distinct output vertices \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), with the input and output sets disjoint. Inputs have indegree zero and outputs have outdegree zero. Intermediate nodes and output nodes compute functions of their incoming values. Fan-in and fan-out are unrestricted; every edge counts as one wire, including edges into output nodes. Unary gates are permitted. The graph has no parallel edges and there is no depth bound. Size counts wires, not gates, truth-table bits, or the time to evaluate the gates.

In the XOR model every noninput node computes the XOR of all its incoming bits, with a zero-input node computing zero. In the GEN model a noninput node of indegree \(k\) may compute any fixed Boolean function \(\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\); this includes unary negation, constants and nonlinear functions. Its input wires are ordered when specifying this function. Gate functions and wiring may depend arbitrarily on \(A\), but not on the input vector beyond the values carried by their specified wires. The gate's truth table is not charged; each value transmitted along a wire is one bit. There are no external oracles, advice inputs, random choices, or correctness promises on the input vector.

Write \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\) and \(C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\) for the respective minimum wire counts of circuits computing every coordinate of \(Ax\) exactly for every \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\). These finite minima are nonuniform circuit quantities; no efficient algorithm producing an optimum from \(A\) is required. For a nonzero matrix both minima are positive, and \(C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\le C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\) because parity is an allowed general gate. Restricting to nonzero matrices avoids undefined ratios. Arbitrary gates of unbounded fan-in are essential to the source's GEN model; replacing them with a fixed binary Boolean basis would change the question.

The positive constant \(K\) is chosen before the dimension and matrix. They may depend on \(K\), and may be obtained by a nonconstructive argument. A negative answer is exactly a finite constant \(K\) for which \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\le K C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\) holds for all dimensions and matrices. Computation only on the unit basis vectors is insufficient: nonlinear circuits need not be determined on other inputs by their behavior on that basis.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated unbounded-ratio assertion. A positive answer must establish arbitrarily large wire savings for some matrices, with no prescribed rate or efficient-generation requirement. A negative answer must establish a universal finite simulation factor for every square matrix. A result only for most matrices, for bounded depth, for gates with a bounded arity or fixed basis, or for correctness solely on a selected set of inputs does not settle the claim. A static data-structure lower bound must be shown to imply the exact unrestricted circuit comparison before it can serve as a resolution. No complexity conjecture is assumed.

context_blocks.text: Chapter 6 defines GEN using arbitrary Boolean gate functions and wire count. The paragraph following Problem 7.18 identifies a constant-factor XOR/GEN bound as a negative answer. Accordingly the target is an unbounded asymptotic advantage, not any finite example with a smaller constant-size circuit.

The source distinguishes full computation of a linear operator from correct behavior only on the unit basis vectors. In the latter relaxed problem, nonlinear gates can offer large savings; for full computation, those values alone do not constrain arbitrary gates on other inputs.

The source relates a universal negative answer to a separate min-rank conjecture about partially specified matrices. That conjectural implication supplies context, not an additional assumption in this card.

Ko’s September 2025 preprint studies nonlinear preprocessing for a fixed linear query family and obtains new bounds for random operators, together with consequences for circuits at fixed depth. Its introduction continues to describe the general nonlinear advantage issue as a longstanding question. Such restricted or typical-matrix lower bounds do not establish a constant-factor comparison for every matrix at unrestricted depth.
